stem:
A 31-year-old teacher is seen after three similar events over two months. Each time, while sitting at her desk, her left hand has started to jerk rhythmically for about a minute while she stayed awake. She was then vague and muddled for several minutes. Her partner has witnessed two of the events and says they looked identical. There was no warning, no trigger, no pallor and no palpitations, and examination between events is normal.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Focal seizure arising from the motor cortex
options.B: Transient ischaemic attack in the carotid territory
options.C: Vasovagal syncope with brief convulsive jerks
options.D: Migraine with aura affecting the hand
options.E: Panic attack with hyperventilation

correct_answer: A. Focal seizure arising from the motor cortex
why_correct: Recurrent identical episodes of rhythmic jerking confined to one limb, with preserved awareness and then a period of post-event confusion, are typical of a focal motor seizure. The pattern points to abnormal electrical activity in one area of cortex rather than a global drop in cerebral perfusion. She needs an urgent specialist (neurology or epilepsy) assessment, with advice about driving. Source: NICE NG217, Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, 2022.
why_wrong: B. A TIA causes sudden negative symptoms such as weakness or numbness, not rhythmic positive jerking. C. Syncope follows a trigger or prodrome with pallor and rapid recovery, and any brief jerks occur after she has lost consciousness. D. Migraine aura spreads gradually over several minutes and causes sensory or visual symptoms rather than rhythmic limb jerking. E. A panic attack brings fear, palpitations and breathlessness, not identical focal limb jerking.
pearl: Stereotyped focal motor jerking followed by post-event confusion is a focal seizure until proven otherwise, and a first episode merits urgent specialist review rather than routine follow-up.
thinking: Identical repeated events  ↓  rhythmic jerking of one hand with awareness retained  ↓  post-event confusion, no trigger or prodrome  ↓  focal seizure  ↓  urgent specialist referral and driving advice.
exam_trap: C, convulsive syncope: brief jerks can occur in a faint, but they follow a prodrome or trigger with pallor and loss of awareness from the start.
takeaway: Stereotyped rhythmic jerking of one limb followed by confusion indicates a focal seizure, so refer for specialist assessment.

Source key was unchanged and sound. Live bank checked: focal seizure items (NEU111, PAQ15459) are temporal-lobe/impaired-awareness; BX665 asks mechanism; none tests simple motor-jerking recognition. stem:
A 62-year-old woman wakes at 06:30 with slurred speech and weakness of her left arm. Her husband says she went to bed at 23:00 and seemed completely normal. The ambulance crew bring her to the emergency department, where the stroke team is activated and a CT head is arranged.

Which piece of history is the most important when deciding whether she can have acute reperfusion treatment?

options.A: When she was last known to be symptom free
options.B: Her family history of heart disease
options.C: How many years she has smoked cigarettes
options.D: Her typical sleep pattern over recent months
options.E: The age at which her menopause began

correct_answer: A. When she was last known to be symptom free
why_correct: Eligibility for thrombolysis and thrombectomy depends on how long ago the stroke started. When onset was not witnessed, as with a wake-up stroke, the clock starts from the time the person was last known to be well, and treatment decisions are then guided by that time and by imaging. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, 2022.
why_wrong: B. Family history helps with long-term prevention but does not decide acute eligibility. C. Smoking history is a risk factor and does not set the treatment window. D. Her sleep habits do not alter how reperfusion eligibility is judged. E. Menopausal history is irrelevant to the acute decision.
pearl: If onset is unwitnessed, including a wake-up stroke, use the last time the patient was known to be well, not the time they were found.
thinking: Symptoms found on waking  ↓  onset unwitnessed  ↓  work out when she was last known to be well  ↓  that time plus imaging guides thrombolysis and thrombectomy.
exam_trap: Using the time she woke up or arrived in hospital as onset underestimates the true interval and can lead to treatment outside its safe window.
takeaway: For unwitnessed onset, always document the last time the patient was known to be well, because it drives reperfusion decisions.
notes: Reangled to an unwitnessed wake-up stroke so the item cannot be answered by guesswork; no timing thresholds are asked. Verified NG128 wording ('last known to be well', wake-up strokes included). Key moved to A per plan. Live bank: NEU048 mentions 'last seen well' but tests thrombolysis; no item on last-known-well. Source key sound.

stem:
A 63-year-old woman is brought in by her daughter after suddenly dropping her cup with her right hand. She then found she could not lift her right leg properly and kept bumping into the doorframe on her right side. She says that she cannot see anything to the right with either eye. Her capillary glucose is normal and she has no headache.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Detached retina affecting the right eye
options.B: Acute stroke from a left-sided lesion
options.C: Optic neuritis with pain on eye movement
options.D: Functional neurological disorder
options.E: Migraine with a typical visual aura

correct_answer: B. Acute stroke from a left-sided lesion
why_correct: Sudden weakness of one arm and leg together with loss of the same side of the visual field in both eyes points to a lesion in the opposite cerebral hemisphere, and in this setting an acute stroke. A normal glucose excludes the commonest mimic. She needs the acute stroke pathway with immediate brain imaging. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, 2022.
why_wrong: A. A detached retina affects one eye only and does not cause limb weakness. C. Optic neuritis affects one eye with pain on movement and causes no limb weakness or field loss in both eyes. D. Functional disorder is a diagnosis of exclusion, and field loss in both eyes with weakness fits a structural lesion. E. Migraine aura develops gradually over minutes, is positive in character and does not usually cause hemiparesis.
pearl: Hemiparesis with a homonymous hemianopia (the same side of the field lost in both eyes) localises to the opposite hemisphere, so right-sided signs mean a left-sided lesion.
thinking: Sudden onset, motor deficit plus visual field loss  ↓  field loss in both eyes means a post-chiasmal lesion  ↓  glucose normal, no mimic  ↓  acute stroke in the opposite hemisphere  ↓  stroke pathway and urgent imaging.
exam_trap: C, optic neuritis: it can look like a sudden visual problem but it is monocular and painful and does not cause weakness.
takeaway: Sudden hemiparesis with a homonymous field defect is a stroke in the opposite hemisphere until proven otherwise.
notes: New vignette (right-sided, 63-year-old woman, glucose checked) replacing the left-sided hemianopia stem; key moved to B per plan; 'opposite cerebral hemisphere' kept as the learning point. Distractors made clinically plausible (retinal, migraine, optic neuritis, functional). stem:
A 29-year-old man notices numbness spreading up from both feet over two days. His legs then become weak and stiff, and since yesterday he has had difficulty starting to pass urine. Examination shows reduced power in both legs, brisk knee and ankle reflexes with upgoing plantar responses, and reduced pinprick sensation below the umbilicus. Arms and cranial nerves are normal.

Which site of the nervous system is most likely to be affected?

options.A: Cauda equina below the level of L1
options.B: Spinal cord at the thoracic level
options.C: Peripheral nerves of both legs
options.D: Neuromuscular junction at the muscles
options.E: Both cerebral hemispheres together

correct_answer: B. Spinal cord at the thoracic level
why_correct: Bilateral leg weakness with upper motor neurone signs (brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars), a sensory level and early bladder dysfunction localises to the spinal cord. Urgent MRI of the spine is needed to look for a compressive cause that would need emergency decompression, and then for inflammatory or other myelopathy. Source: NICE NG234, Spinal metastases and metastatic spinal cord compression, 2023 (urgent MRI principle); clinical neuroanatomy.
why_wrong: A. Cauda equina lesions give lower motor neurone signs with reduced reflexes and saddle numbness rather than a sensory level and brisk reflexes. C. Peripheral nerve disease causes reduced reflexes and a stocking pattern without a sensory level. D. Neuromuscular junction disease causes fatigable weakness with normal sensation. E. Bilateral hemispheric disease would affect cognition, arms and cranial nerves.
pearl: A sensory level with brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars and bladder involvement means spinal cord until proven otherwise, and needs urgent spinal MRI.
thinking: Both legs weak and stiff  ↓  brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars  ↓  sensory level below the umbilicus plus urinary hesitancy  ↓  spinal cord lesion  ↓  urgent MRI spine.
exam_trap: A, cauda equina: it also causes bilateral leg weakness and urinary retention, but reflexes are reduced and there is no sensory level.
takeaway: A sensory level with upper motor neurone signs in the legs and bladder dysfunction localises to the spinal cord and needs urgent MRI.
notes: Reangled from 'concern: spinal cord compression' (AKT diagnosis) to localisation to the spinal cord, because a 29-year-old with no cancer or trauma history may have a compressive or non-compressive myelopathy; the urgent-MRI message is kept in the explanation. Added UMN signs and level so the item is unambiguous (source stem lacked reflexes). Key moved to B per plan. stem:
A 66-year-old woman was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease by a specialist three years ago and takes co-careldopa. She asks why she has had long-standing constipation, has lost her sense of smell and sometimes shouts out and moves her arms in her sleep. Her bowel habit has otherwise been stable and she has no weight loss or rectal bleeding.

How are these symptoms best described?

options.A: Unrelated age-related changes that are not part of her condition
options.B: Adverse effects of her levodopa that need the drug stopped at once
options.C: Features of a second neurodegenerative disorder developing alongside
options.D: Warning signs of a bowel tumour needing urgent cancer pathway referral
options.E: Recognised non-motor manifestations of Parkinson's disease itself

correct_answer: E. Recognised non-motor manifestations of Parkinson's disease itself
why_correct: Parkinson's disease is more than a movement disorder. Constipation, loss of smell (hyposmia), disturbed sleep including REM sleep behaviour disorder, low mood and autonomic problems are well-recognised non-motor features, and several can precede the tremor and slowness. Recognising them allows each to be asked about and treated. Source: NICE NG71, Parkinson's disease in adults, 2017 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. Attributing them to ageing misses treatable features of the disease. B. Levodopa can cause nausea and hypotension, but loss of smell and dream enactment are not drug effects, and stopping it abruptly is dangerous. C. Nothing suggests a second disorder, as these symptoms are part of the Parkinson's picture. D. A stable bowel habit without red-flag features does not suggest bowel cancer.
pearl: Hyposmia, constipation and REM sleep behaviour disorder can appear years before the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease.
thinking: Known Parkinson's disease  ↓  constipation, anosmia and dream enactment  ↓  none are motor signs  ↓  no red flags for bowel malignancy  ↓  non-motor features of the disease.
exam_trap: Choosing the cancer-pathway option because of constipation, when the habit is stable and there are no alarm features.
takeaway: Constipation, loss of smell and sleep disturbance are recognised non-motor features of Parkinson's disease, not separate problems.
notes: Rewritten as a vignette with REM sleep behaviour disorder added as a third non-motor feature and red-flag absence stated; key unchanged (non-motor manifestations). Source was a bare one-liner. stem:
A 24-year-old man has struggled with falling asleep at work for the past year. His girlfriend notices that when he laughs hard at a joke his jaw sags and his knees give way so that he slides to the floor. The episodes last a few seconds. He says he heard everything that was said throughout and he is back to normal straight away.

Which description best fits these episodes?

options.A: Rhythmic jerking of all four limbs followed by prolonged drowsiness
options.B: Sudden blank staring with loss of awareness but no loss of posture
options.C: A faint caused by a fall in blood pressure when he stands up
options.D: Transient one-sided weakness with slurred speech lasting minutes
options.E: Brief loss of muscle tone while his awareness is fully preserved

correct_answer: E. Brief loss of muscle tone while his awareness is fully preserved
why_correct: These are episodes of cataplexy, a sudden, brief loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion such as laughter, and it is characteristic of narcolepsy type 1. Awareness is retained throughout and recovery is immediate, which separates it from seizures and syncope. Source: NICE CKS, Narcolepsy, 2023; International Classification of Sleep Disorders.
why_wrong: A. Tonic-clonic seizures cause loss of awareness and a prolonged post-ictal period. B. Absence seizures cause loss of awareness with staring but do not cause collapse. C. Postural syncope follows standing and involves loss of awareness, not an emotional trigger. D. Transient one-sided weakness with speech disturbance describes a transient ischaemic attack and needs urgent assessment.
pearl: Cataplexy is triggered by positive emotion such as laughter, and the person stays aware throughout.
thinking: Emotional trigger  ↓  seconds of collapsing tone  ↓  awareness preserved with immediate recovery  ↓  cataplexy, not seizure or syncope.
exam_trap: Calling the episodes seizures because of the collapse, when awareness is preserved and there is no post-ictal period.
takeaway: Cataplexy is brief emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness.
notes: Source was a bare one-line feature question; built a vignette and asked for the best description. Live PAQ15793 asks for the diagnosis (narcolepsy) from a similar picture, so the learning point here (what cataplexy looks like versus seizure, syncope and TIA) is a distinct angle, but a reviewer may judge it too close. stem:
A 70-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation suddenly develops weakness of her left face and left arm, with the leg only mildly affected. She does not look to her left, ignores food on the left side of her plate and says there is nothing wrong with her. Her speech is clear.

Which arterial territory is most likely to be affected?

options.A: Left middle cerebral artery
options.B: Right anterior cerebral artery
options.C: Right middle cerebral artery
options.D: Left posterior cerebral artery
options.E: Basilar artery

correct_answer: C. Right middle cerebral artery
why_correct: Face and arm weakness greater than leg weakness points to the middle cerebral artery territory, because the leg area lies on the medial surface supplied by the anterior cerebral artery. Neglect of the left side of space with lack of insight is a non-dominant (usually right) parietal sign, and the weakness is on the opposite side to the lesion, so the right middle cerebral artery is affected. Clear speech makes a dominant-hemisphere lesion less likely. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, 2022; Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine.
why_wrong: A. A left middle cerebral lesion would give right-sided weakness and usually aphasia. B. Anterior cerebral occlusion causes leg weakness greater than arm weakness, which is the reverse of this pattern. D. A left posterior cerebral lesion causes a right visual field defect, not left hemiparesis with neglect. E. Basilar occlusion causes brainstem signs such as reduced consciousness and bilateral deficits.
pearl: In middle cerebral stroke the arm and face are hit harder than the leg, and the side of the neglect tells you the hemisphere.
thinking: Left face and arm weakness  ↓  leg relatively spared, so not anterior cerebral  ↓  left neglect with preserved speech  ↓  right (non-dominant) hemisphere  ↓  right middle cerebral artery.
exam_trap: Matching the side of the weakness to the same-side artery instead of the opposite hemisphere.
takeaway: Face and arm weakness worse than leg weakness with contralateral neglect localises to the non-dominant middle cerebral artery territory.
notes: New vignette (AF cardioembolic setting, lack of insight, preserved speech) replacing the source's description; options reworded and reordered, key unchanged (right MCA). Live PAQ16161 is LEFT MCA with aphasia and BX879 asks only which hemisphere causes neglect, so this is a different question (artery localisation by limb pattern plus neglect side). Standard stroke localisation; NICE NG128 cited for stroke pathway generally.

stem:
A 48-year-old woman wakes with weakness of the whole of the right side of her face, including her forehead. Bell's palsy is diagnosed and she starts oral prednisolone. Her right eye does not close fully when she blinks or sleeps, and it waters in the day. She is advised to use lubricating eye drops and to tape the eye closed at night.

What is the main eye complication this advice aims to prevent?

options.A: Raised intraocular pressure causing acute glaucoma
options.B: Retinal detachment from facial muscle traction
options.C: Optic nerve inflammation causing visual loss
options.D: Lens opacity developing from steroid treatment
options.E: Corneal drying and ulceration from lid exposure

correct_answer: E. Corneal drying and ulceration from lid exposure
why_correct: Facial nerve weakness stops the eyelid closing properly, so the cornea is exposed and dries, especially overnight. This risks keratopathy, ulceration and permanent visual damage, so eye protection with lubricating drops by day, ointment and taping at night is advised from the start, with prompt ophthalmology review if the eye becomes painful or red. Source: NICE CKS, Bell's palsy, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Angle-closure glaucoma is not caused by facial palsy. B. Retinal detachment is unrelated to the facial nerve or the eyelid muscles. C. Optic neuritis involves the optic nerve, not the facial nerve. D. Cataract from steroids needs prolonged high-dose use, not a short course, and is not the aim of eye protection.
pearl: The patient cannot protect the cornea if the blink and lid closure are lost, so protect it for them.
thinking: Facial nerve palsy  ↓  incomplete eyelid closure  ↓  cornea exposed and dry  ↓  lubricate by day, tape and ointment at night  ↓  prevent exposure keratopathy.
exam_trap: Choosing the steroid-related cataract because the patient is on prednisolone.
takeaway: In Bell's palsy the eye needs active protection because incomplete closure exposes the cornea to damage.
notes: Source was a bare one-liner; built a vignette so that the key is exposure of the cornea. stem:
A 69-year-old woman is helped into her GP surgery by her daughter. Forty minutes ago her mouth drooped on the right, her right arm became weak and her speech turned slurred. She is alert and the signs are still present.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Call 999 for emergency transfer to a hyper-acute stroke unit
options.B: Arrange an urgent outpatient CT head scan within the week
options.C: Give aspirin and refer to the next available TIA clinic
options.D: Observe in the surgery for a few hours to see if the signs settle
options.E: Request a routine neurology outpatient review for new weakness

correct_answer: A. Call 999 for emergency transfer to a hyper-acute stroke unit
why_correct: Sudden face, arm and speech problems that persist are a positive FAST screen and mean acute stroke until proven otherwise. NICE advises that people with suspected stroke are transferred immediately by emergency ambulance to a specialist acute stroke unit, where urgent brain imaging decides on thrombolysis or thrombectomy. Treatment benefit falls with every minute of delay. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, 2019.
why_wrong: B. An outpatient scan within the week would miss the window for reperfusion treatment and gives no immediate assessment. C. Aspirin must not be given before haemorrhage is excluded on imaging, and a TIA clinic is for symptoms that have fully resolved. D. Waiting wastes the treatment window, and even if signs resolved she would still need urgent TIA assessment. E. A routine neurology appointment is far too slow for an acute focal deficit.
pearl: Face, Arm, Speech, Time: any persisting FAST feature means a 999 call, not a surgery or outpatient pathway.
thinking: Sudden face, arm and speech deficit  ↓  Positive FAST, acute stroke until proven otherwise  ↓  Time-critical reperfusion options  ↓  999 transfer to hyper-acute stroke unit
exam_trap: Choosing aspirin or observation in the surgery feels cautious but delays imaging and reperfusion decisions.

A 41-year-old man wakes with weakness of the whole of the right side of his face, including the forehead. There are no limb or speech problems and no rash. When he tries to shut his right eye it stays partly open, and it is red and watering. Oral prednisolone is started.

Which additional measure is most appropriate to protect the eye?

options.A: Topical antibiotic ointment applied routinely to the affected eye
options.B: A firm eye pad kept in place continuously, day and night
options.C: Early referral for surgical suturing of the eyelids
options.D: Lubricating drops by day and ointment with taping at night
options.E: No specific eye care, as the palsy is expected to recover fully

correct_answer: D. Lubricating drops by day and ointment with taping at night
why_correct: Failure of eyelid closure in a lower motor neurone facial palsy exposes the cornea, which can dry out, ulcerate and scar. Eye care is therefore part of initial management: regular lubricating drops during the day, and ointment with gentle taping of the lid at night. Pain, redness or visual change should prompt same-day ophthalmology review. Source: NICE CKS, Bell's palsy, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are only needed if there is infection, not as routine prophylaxis for exposure. B. A tight pad can abrade an incompletely closed eye and hides early warning signs. C. Surgical eyelid closure is reserved for severe or persistent cases under ophthalmology, not initial care. E. Recovery is likely, but the cornea can be damaged before it occurs.
pearl: The risk in Bell's palsy is to the eye, not just the face: protect the cornea from the first day.
thinking: Lower motor neurone facial palsy  ↓  Eyelid cannot close  ↓  Exposure keratopathy risk  ↓  Lubricate by day, ointment and tape at night
exam_trap: Assuming a self-limiting palsy needs no eye care, or reaching for patching or antibiotics instead of lubrication.
takeaway: In facial palsy with incomplete eye closure, lubricate and protect the cornea, and refer early if the eye becomes painful or red.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman reports that she copes well with stairs in the morning but struggles by the evening. Her arms tire when brushing her hair, and her voice becomes quieter and slurred if she reads aloud for a few minutes. Resting for a while helps. Tone, reflexes and sensation are normal, and her creatine kinase is normal.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Polymyositis
options.B: Guillain-Barré syndrome
options.C: Myasthenia gravis
options.D: Motor neurone disease
options.E: Multiple sclerosis

correct_answer: C. Myasthenia gravis
why_correct: Weakness that builds with repeated or sustained activity, including bulbar fatigue, and recovers with rest is the hallmark of myasthenia gravis, an antibody-mediated disorder of the neuromuscular junction. Reflexes and sensation are typically preserved and creatine kinase is normal. Diagnosis is supported by acetylcholine receptor antibodies, with further tests if these are negative. Source: NICE CKS, Myasthenia gravis, and Association of British Neurologists guidance.
why_wrong: A. Polymyositis causes painless proximal weakness with a raised creatine kinase, without fatigability. B. Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending weakness with reduced reflexes over days, not weakness that varies through the day. D. Motor neurone disease causes progressive weakness with mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs, not recovery with rest. E. Multiple sclerosis causes relapsing deficits separated in time and place, not weakness that recovers within minutes of rest.
pearl: Fatigability with recovery on rest points to the neuromuscular junction, not to muscle or nerve.
thinking: Weakness worse with use, better with rest  ↓  Bulbar and proximal involvement, normal reflexes and CK  ↓  Neuromuscular junction disorder  ↓  Myasthenia gravis
exam_trap: Choosing polymyositis because of proximal weakness, forgetting that fatigability and a normal creatine kinase point elsewhere.
takeaway: Fatigable proximal and bulbar weakness that improves with rest, with normal reflexes and sensation, is myasthenia gravis until proven otherwise.
notes: New vignette adds bulbar fatigue and normal CK/reflexes; non-ocular presentation chosen to avoid duplicating live ocular items (NEU022, BX070, PAQ16007). Source's 'peripheral arterial disease' and 'Parkinson's' distractors replaced with neuromuscular differentials. No figures. Citation is general (CKS geo-blocked); clinical content standard. Also stands in for PAN8595 (neuromuscular junction site).
Bare one-line recall (myasthenia gravis affects the neuromuscular junction); same learning area as my PAN5158 and adds nothing as a separate question.

stem:
A 55-year-old man has had right-sided sciatica for several weeks. A physiotherapist notices that his right foot slaps down onto the floor with each step and that he lifts the knee unusually high to avoid catching his toes.

Which movement is weak?

options.A: Pushing the foot downwards at the ankle
options.B: Straightening the knee against resistance
options.C: Pulling the foot upwards at the ankle
options.D: Curling the toes downwards
options.E: Extending the hip backwards

correct_answer: C. Pulling the foot upwards at the ankle
why_correct: This is foot drop, a weakness of ankle dorsiflexion produced by tibialis anterior and the other anterior compartment muscles. The toes drag during the swing phase, so the patient lifts the knee high (a steppage gait) and the foot slaps down. A common cause is an L5 radiculopathy, as here, or a common fibular nerve lesion. New foot drop needs a prompt neurological assessment to find the level of the lesion. Source: NICE CKS, Sciatica (lumbar radiculopathy), 2023.
why_wrong: A. Ankle plantarflexion is supplied through the tibial nerve and is usually preserved in foot drop. B. Knee extension depends on the femoral nerve (L3 and L4) and is not the defining deficit. D. Toe flexion is a different motor deficit and does not cause the swing-phase problem. E. Hip extension weakness produces a different gait problem, such as difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs.
pearl: Foot drop is a problem of lifting the front of the foot, so look for a high-stepping gait and foot slap.
thinking: High-stepping gait with foot slap  ↓  Toes cannot clear the floor  ↓  Ankle dorsiflexion weak  ↓  Foot drop
exam_trap: Describing the gait fault in terms of plantarflexion or hip weakness because the leg looks 'weak' overall.
takeaway: Foot drop means weak ankle dorsiflexion; identify whether the cause is nerve root or peripheral nerve.
notes: Re-built a bare recall item into a short vignette; same fact (foot drop = weak dorsiflexion). Cause kept to L5 radiculopathy so the item does not overlap NEU087 (common fibular nerve lesion) or BX983/BX1058 (which root). Options written as descriptions of movements. CKS Sciatica site geo-blocked; content standard.

stem:
A 66-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes reports unsteadiness, particularly in the dark or when washing his face with his eyes shut. When he stands with his feet together he is steady with his eyes open, but he sways and nearly falls once he closes them. Power and tone are normal.

Which deficit best explains this finding?

options.A: Loss of peripheral vision in both eyes
options.B: Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion on both sides
options.C: Cerebellar vermis damage causing truncal ataxia
options.D: Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss
options.E: Impaired joint position sense in both feet

correct_answer: E. Impaired joint position sense in both feet
why_correct: Balance relies on vision, vestibular input and proprioception. A patient who is steady with the eyes open but unstable on eye closure (a positive Romberg test) has lost joint position sense and is relying on vision to compensate, as in a diabetic sensory neuropathy or dorsal column disease. Cerebellar disease causes unsteadiness whether the eyes are open or shut. Source: NICE CKS, Diabetes - type 2 (neuropathy), 2023.
why_wrong: A. Visual field loss would not make him unsafe specifically when the eyes are closed. B. Weakness would make him unsteady regardless of eye closure and his power is normal. C. Cerebellar ataxia is present with the eyes open as well and is not corrected by vision. D. Hearing loss does not impair balance in this way.
pearl: Unsteady with the eyes shut and steady with the eyes open means a sensory (proprioceptive) problem, not a cerebellar one.
thinking: Steady eyes open, falls eyes closed  ↓  Positive Romberg sign  ↓  Proprioceptive loss in the feet  ↓  Sensory ataxia
exam_trap: Calling every unsteady gait cerebellar; a cerebellar patient is unsteady with the eyes open too.
takeaway: A positive Romberg sign indicates loss of proprioception (sensory ataxia).
notes: Vignette adds diabetes and an explicit Romberg description; same fact as source (worse with eyes closed = proprioceptive loss). Cerebellar distractor deliberately included to teach the contrast. Closest live items (BX175/BX340 cerebellum, NEU112 B12) test different localising points. CKS geo-blocked; content standard examination teaching.
Duplicates live NEU073 and GER031 (normal pressure hydrocephalus triad).
Same learning point (Parkinson's hallucinations: look for medical/drug triggers first) as my PAN224; also live PAQ15469/PAQ16456.

stem:
A 79-year-old woman has had Parkinson's disease for eight years. She tells her GP that she occasionally sees a cat on the sofa that is not there. She knows it is not real, is not troubled by it, and her husband is relaxed about it. Her medicines have not changed for two years and she is otherwise well.

What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Start low-dose olanzapine to stop the symptoms progressing
options.B: Stop her co-careldopa until the hallucinations have settled
options.C: Start low-dose haloperidol each evening to suppress the symptoms
options.D: Start low-dose quetiapine and review in a month's time
options.E: Check for medical triggers; do not treat tolerated symptoms

correct_answer: E. Check for medical triggers; do not treat tolerated symptoms
why_correct: NICE advises a general medical evaluation for anyone with Parkinson's hallucinations and treatment of any trigger found, such as infection. If the hallucinations are well tolerated by the patient and family, they should not be treated. Treatment is considered only if they become distressing, and then involves specialist-guided dose reduction and quetiapine or clozapine. Source: NICE NG71, Parkinson's disease in adults, 2017 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. Olanzapine should not be offered for Parkinson's psychosis because it worsens motor function. B. Dopaminergic treatment must not be withdrawn abruptly because of the risk of acute akinesia or a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome. C. Haloperidol and other dopamine-blocking antipsychotics can severely worsen parkinsonism. D. Quetiapine is an option for distressing symptoms but is not needed when they are tolerated.
pearl: Tolerated hallucinations in Parkinson's disease do not need an antipsychotic; look for a trigger first.
thinking: Parkinson's disease with insightful visual hallucinations  ↓  Medical or drug trigger?  ↓  Tolerated by patient and family  ↓  Do not treat
exam_trap: Reaching for an antipsychotic or stopping dopaminergic drugs when the hallucinations are not distressing.
takeaway: Evaluate for triggers, and withhold treatment if hallucinations are well tolerated.
notes: NG71 recommendations 1.5.13-1.5.20 checked (general medical evaluation; do not treat if well tolerated; reduce triggering drugs with specialist advice; quetiapine/clozapine; do not offer olanzapine; other antipsychotics worsen motor features). Quetiapine made a distractor (reasonable only for distressing symptoms). Sibling items PAN1236 and PAN640 skipped as the same learning point. Distinct from PAQ15469/PAQ16456 (cause of hallucinations after ropinirole) and COE006 (Lewy body, avoid antipsychotics).
Same learning point (Parkinson's hallucinations after medication change: review medication and medical causes) as my PAN224; also live PAQ15469/PAQ16456.
Duplicates live PAQ15497 (little-finger numbness, elbow resting -> ulnar nerve); also NEU088.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has had night-time tingling in her thumb and next two fingers for years. She now drops cups and cannot open jars. The fleshy pad at the base of her thumb looks flattened, and she cannot bring her thumb across to touch her little fingertip.

Which muscles are wasted?

options.A: Muscles of the hypothenar eminence
options.B: Short muscles of the thenar eminence
options.C: Dorsal interosseous muscles of the hand
options.D: Extensor muscles of the posterior forearm
options.E: Flexor muscles of the upper arm

correct_answer: B. Short muscles of the thenar eminence
why_correct: In long-standing carpal tunnel syndrome, compression of the median nerve at the wrist can damage its recurrent motor branch, which supplies the thenar muscles that abduct, flex and oppose the thumb. Wasting of the thenar eminence with weak opposition indicates advanced compression. Thenar wasting or weakness is a reason to refer for consideration of surgical decompression rather than continuing conservative treatment. Source: NICE CKS, Carpal tunnel syndrome, 2023.
why_wrong: A. The hypothenar muscles move the little finger and are supplied by the ulnar nerve. C. The interossei abduct and adduct the fingers and are supplied by the ulnar nerve. D. The forearm extensors are supplied by the radial nerve and are not affected in carpal tunnel syndrome. E. The upper arm flexors are supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, above the level of the lesion.
pearl: Thenar wasting in carpal tunnel syndrome means motor involvement and a need for surgical referral.
thinking: Median nerve compression at the wrist  ↓  Recurrent motor branch  ↓  Thumb opposition weak  ↓  Thenar muscles wasted
exam_trap: Confusing thenar (median) with hypothenar (ulnar) muscles; the thumb side is median.
takeaway: Carpal tunnel syndrome with thumb weakness or wasting involves the thenar muscles and warrants surgical referral.
notes: Re-angled the bare 'which muscle group' recall into a clinical picture with wasting, adding the referral implication (thenar wasting/weakness as a surgical referral trigger per CKS). Distractors changed to varied muscle groups with different nerve supplies; source's 'triceps' and 'deltoid' replaced. Near live items (RHE002, BX069, BX1015) test diagnosis/nerve/splinting, not motor involvement. CKS geo-blocked; content standard.
Skip: live BX173 (wasting, fasciculations, slow weakness -> lower motor neurone lesion) already tests the same learning point; NEU070 also covers MND.
Skip: live BX659 already tests meningism developing after thunderclap onset (SAH).

stem:
A 34-year-old man has had a foul-smelling discharge from his left ear on and off for years. Over the past week he has developed a worsening headache, fevers, vomiting and clumsiness of his left hand. He is drowsy and has a left-sided intention tremor.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Chronic subdural haematoma
options.B: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
options.C: Migraine with brainstem aura
options.D: Intracranial abscess of ear origin
options.E: Acute angle-closure glaucoma attack

correct_answer: D. Intracranial abscess of ear origin
why_correct: Long-standing chronic ear disease can spread to the adjacent temporal lobe or cerebellum, forming an abscess. The combination of headache, fever, vomiting, drowsiness and a focal cerebellar sign points to a space-occupying intracranial infection, which needs urgent imaging and neurosurgical and microbiology input. Source: NICE CKS, Otitis media - chronic suppurative (complications), 2022.
why_wrong: A. A chronic subdural haematoma follows head injury in older or anticoagulated patients and does not cause fever. B. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension occurs in young obese women with papilloedema and does not cause fever or focal signs. C. Migraine with brainstem aura causes transient symptoms with full recovery and is not febrile. E. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a painful red eye with visual loss, not fever with cerebellar signs.
pearl: Ear, sinus, dental and heart infections are the usual sources of a brain abscess, so always ask about them in headache with fever.
thinking: Headache plus fever plus focal deficit  ↓  Look for a source: chronic ear disease  ↓  Intracranial abscess likely  ↓  Urgent contrast imaging and specialist referral
exam_trap: Treating this as migraine or a simple infective illness because the headache is the main complaint delays imaging and neurosurgical input.
takeaway: Fever, headache and a new focal neurological sign in someone with chronic ear infection is an intracranial abscess until proved otherwise.
notes: Source stem asked 'what diagnosis should be considered' with a bare otitis media history; rebuilt around a cerebellar sign and drowsiness. PAN3828 (endocarditis source, same learning point) skipped to avoid repeating. Live DF001 tests imaging after a dental source; this tests recognition of an ear-origin abscess.
Skip: live BX664/NEU118 already test raised ICP from headache/vomiting (worse in the morning) in mass lesions.
Skip: live PAN7492 already tests photophobia as a migraine accompaniment (also a bare one-line recall item).

stem:
A 24-year-old woman has had several throbbing headaches over the past year, each starting on one side and lasting about half a day. During attacks she feels sick, cannot tolerate bright light and prefers to lie in a dark room. She has no visual symptoms beforehand, is entirely well between attacks, and her neurological examination is normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Cluster headache
options.B: Tension-type headache
options.C: Medication-overuse headache
options.D: Giant cell arteritis
options.E: Migraine without aura

correct_answer: E. Migraine without aura
why_correct: Recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches lasting hours, with nausea and sensitivity to light, and complete recovery between attacks, fit migraine without aura. The normal examination and absence of red flags make a secondary cause unlikely. Source: NICE CKS, Migraine - diagnosis, 2024; NICE CG150, Headaches in over 12s, 2012.
why_wrong: A. Cluster headache causes short, very severe orbital pain with ipsilateral tearing and restlessness, mostly in men. B. Tension-type headache is bilateral, pressing and not accompanied by nausea or marked photophobia. C. Medication-overuse headache is a near-daily headache in someone taking acute analgesics frequently. D. Giant cell arteritis affects people over 50 and causes scalp tenderness and jaw claudication.
pearl: Migraine is a clinical diagnosis: a stereotyped attack with nausea and photophobia and a normal examination between attacks needs no imaging.
thinking: Recurrent stereotyped headaches  ↓  Unilateral, throbbing, nausea, photophobia  ↓  Normal between attacks, no red flags  ↓  Migraine without aura
exam_trap: Over-investigating a typical migraine, or missing that aura is not required for the diagnosis.
takeaway: Recurrent throbbing unilateral headache with nausea and photophobia and a normal examination is migraine; aura is not needed.
notes: Source and PAN766 are both migraine-diagnosis items; PAN766 skipped as a within-batch repeat. Vignette rebuilt (female, attack duration and normal examination added).
Skip: repeat of the migraine-diagnosis learning point written in PAN7586 within this file; PAQ14929/BX022/NEU010 cover migraine too.

Skip: live BX631 and BX335 already test cluster headache/trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia with ipsilateral autonomic features.
Skip: same learning point (brain abscess with fever and focal deficit) already written in PAN3345 within this file; live DF001 also close.
Skip: live BX664, PAN4260 and NEU118 already test headache with vomiting/drowsiness as raised ICP; source is a bare combination-recall item.

stem:
A 66-year-old woman with untreated atrial fibrillation suddenly develops weakness and numbness of her left face, arm and leg. She also fails to notice objects on her left side. Her speech is clear and she remains alert.

Which arterial territory is most likely to be involved?

options.A: Left middle cerebral artery
options.B: Right anterior cerebral artery
options.C: Right posterior cerebral artery
options.D: Right middle cerebral artery
options.E: Vertebrobasilar circulation

correct_answer: D. Right middle cerebral artery
why_correct: The motor, sensory and visual pathways cross, so left-sided face and limb weakness with sensory loss and left visual field loss arises from the right hemisphere. A cardio-embolic occlusion of the right middle cerebral artery supplies the cortex and internal capsule responsible for these deficits. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, 2022.
why_wrong: A. A left middle cerebral lesion would cause right-sided deficits, usually with aphasia. B. Anterior cerebral occlusion mainly weakens the contralateral leg and causes personality change. C. Posterior cerebral occlusion mainly causes a contralateral visual field defect with little weakness. E. Vertebrobasilar disease produces brainstem and cerebellar signs such as vertigo, diplopia and crossed deficits.
pearl: A cortical syndrome of contralateral face and arm weakness, sensory loss and field loss, with or without aphasia or neglect, usually means the middle cerebral artery.
thinking: Left-sided deficit  ↓  Lesion is in the opposite (right) hemisphere  ↓  Face, arm, leg, sensory and field loss  ↓  Right middle cerebral artery
exam_trap: Choosing the side of the body instead of the side of the brain.
takeaway: Stroke deficits are contralateral to the lesion, and a combined motor, sensory and visual field deficit points to the middle cerebral artery territory.
notes: Source key retained (MCA). Implausible options 'Basilar artery necessarily', 'radial artery' and 'optic nerve only' replaced with other cerebral territories. Live PAQ16161 (left MCA with aphasia) and BX879 (right hemisphere neglect) overlap partly but test different laterality and localisation.
Skip: live NEU116 already tests Huntington disease chorea.

stem:
A 17-year-old girl reports that for several months she has had sudden, brief jerks of both arms, usually within an hour of waking, which have made her drop cups at breakfast. She stays fully alert and can describe each episode afterwards. She is otherwise well and has a normal examination.

Which seizure type is she most likely to be having?

options.A: Absence seizure
options.B: Focal impaired-awareness seizure
options.C: Myoclonic seizure
options.D: Atonic seizure
options.E: Tonic-clonic seizure

correct_answer: C. Myoclonic seizure
why_correct: Brief, shock-like jerks of the limbs on waking with preserved awareness are myoclonic seizures, typical of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy which begins in adolescence. This should prompt referral to a specialist in epilepsy for confirmation with an EEG. Source: NICE NG217, Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Absence seizures are brief lapses of awareness with staring and no jerks. B. Focal impaired-awareness seizures cause altered awareness with automatisms. D. Atonic seizures cause a sudden loss of tone and falls rather than jerks. E. Tonic-clonic seizures cause loss of consciousness with sustained stiffening then rhythmic jerking.
pearl: Early-morning jerks with preserved awareness in an adolescent suggest juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, where sleep deprivation and alcohol are triggers.
thinking: Brief muscle jerks on waking  ↓  Awareness preserved  ↓  Adolescent onset  ↓  Myoclonic seizure
exam_trap: Assuming any seizure causes loss of awareness, which would point wrongly to a tonic-clonic or focal seizure.
takeaway: Brief sudden muscle jerks with preserved awareness, especially soon after waking, are myoclonic seizures.
notes: Seizure-type recognition kept as the learning point; vignette changed to an adolescent with functional impact. Not live as a diagnostic item (only JME contraception/valproate items exist).
Skip: live NEU091 already tests restless legs syndrome.

stem:
A 38-year-old man attends his GP surgery with four days of tingling in his feet followed by weakness of both legs. He now needs to hold the banister to climb stairs. He had a diarrhoeal illness two weeks ago. Examination shows symmetrical leg weakness and absent ankle reflexes, with normal speech and swallowing.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Request nerve conduction studies through the routine neurology outpatient service
options.B: Start oral prednisolone and review in the practice clinic after a week
options.C: Check vitamin B12, thyroid function and creatine kinase, then review in a fortnight
options.D: Refer immediately for hospital neurological assessment with respiratory monitoring
options.E: Refer to community physiotherapy and recheck muscle strength after a month

correct_answer: D. Refer immediately for hospital neurological assessment with respiratory monitoring
why_correct: Rapidly progressive symmetrical weakness over days with areflexia after an infection suggests Guillain-Barre syndrome, which can quickly cause respiratory and bulbar failure. NICE advises immediate referral for neurological assessment, where forced vital capacity and swallowing can be monitored. Source: NICE NG127, Suspected neurological conditions: recognition and referral, 2019.
why_wrong: A. Routine outpatient nerve studies would leave a potentially life-threatening condition unmonitored. B. Corticosteroids do not help Guillain-Barre syndrome and the delay is unsafe. C. Waiting a fortnight for blood tests risks respiratory failure in the meantime. E. Physiotherapy and a month's delay is not appropriate for evolving paralysis.
pearl: Speed of progression decides the urgency: weakness developing over days warrants same-day hospital assessment even when the patient is currently walking.
thinking: Symmetrical weakness progressing over days  ↓  Areflexia, recent diarrhoea  ↓  Possible Guillain-Barre syndrome  ↓  Immediate hospital assessment
exam_trap: Being reassured because breathing and swallowing are currently normal, when deterioration can be rapid.
takeaway: Rapidly progressive symmetrical weakness needs immediate referral for neurological assessment, because respiratory failure can develop quickly.
notes: Source said 'over three weeks'; NG127 1.10.2 specifies progression within hours to days, so the timeline was changed to four days. Key is the referral-urgency principle, distinct from live BX426/NEU102/NEU021 (diagnosis, treatment, FVC monitoring). PAN1695 (GBS recognition) skipped as duplicate of BX426.
Skip: live BX426, BX638, PAQ15899 and NEU020 already test recognition of ascending weakness after diarrhoea as Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Skip: live ACU018, NEU048, NEU004 and PAAKT041 already test activating the stroke pathway / urgent imaging and thrombolysis for sudden hemiparesis with dysphasia within hours.
Skip: live BX171, NEU065 and PAAKT044 already test a transient resolved focal deficit as suspected TIA with aspirin and 24-hour assessment.
Skip: live P054, NEU040 and PAAKT165 already test functional neurological disorder with inconsistent weakness.

stem:
A 45-year-old man is an inpatient with Guillain-Barre syndrome. On the sixth day his heart rate swings between slow and very fast and his blood pressure alternates between low and high readings within the same day. He is afebrile, blood cultures are negative and he is not on any new drugs.

Which complication best explains these findings?

options.A: Superimposed cerebellar involvement
options.B: Rising intracranial pressure
options.C: Pulmonary embolism
options.D: Autonomic nerve involvement
options.E: Adrenal insufficiency

correct_answer: D. Autonomic nerve involvement
why_correct: Guillain-Barre syndrome can affect autonomic fibres, causing labile blood pressure, arrhythmias and heart rate swings that may need intensive care monitoring. Once sepsis, drugs and volume problems are excluded, dysautonomia is the likely explanation. Source: NICE CKS, Guillain-Barre syndrome, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Cerebellar involvement causes ataxia and incoordination, not fluctuating cardiovascular parameters. B. Raised intracranial pressure causes headache and drowsiness, typically with a slow heart rate and high blood pressure. C. Pulmonary embolism causes breathlessness and hypoxia rather than alternating swings in rate and pressure. E. Adrenal insufficiency causes sustained hypotension, not alternating high and low values.
pearl: Unstable heart rate and blood pressure in Guillain-Barre syndrome is dysautonomia and is a reason for continuous cardiac monitoring.
thinking: Guillain-Barre syndrome  ↓  Swinging heart rate and blood pressure  ↓  No sepsis or drug cause  ↓  Autonomic dysfunction
exam_trap: Looking for sepsis or embolism alone and missing that the neuropathy itself affects autonomic nerves.
takeaway: Autonomic instability is a recognised complication of Guillain-Barre syndrome and needs close monitoring.
notes: Source key retained; vignette adds exclusion of sepsis and drugs. Implausible distractors (optic neuritis, peripheral vascular disease, raised intraocular pressure) replaced with clinically competing causes.
Skip: live BX171, NEU065 and PAAKT044 already test a resolved 20-minute focal deficit as suspected TIA; also repeats PAN317 learning point.
Skip: bare recall that sudden-onset focal deficit means stroke; live BX884, BX627 and BX880 already test acute stroke recognition.
Skip: live NEU004 and PAQ15895 already test non-contrast CT head as the first investigation in suspected acute stroke.
Duplicate: live BX171 (near-identical 70-year-old, arm weakness and speech, fully resolves within 30 minutes) and NEU065 already test suspected TIA needing aspirin and urgent specialist assessment.
Duplicate: live BX170 (focal weakness with low capillary glucose, correct the hypoglycaemia) tests the same stroke-mimic learning point.

Same learning point as PAN8556 (sudden focal deficit = suspected stroke needing urgent action), which is written in this set; avoiding a repeat within W5. Live bank also has NEU004/NEU068 and BX1004 on stroke and the combined pill.

presentation: Sudden face and arm weakness reported in primary care
stem:
A 68-year-old woman is brought to her GP surgery by her husband after she woke with a drooping face and a weak left arm 40 minutes ago. The receptionist noticed that her speech sounded slurred. She is alert and her observations are stable.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Arrange an outpatient CT head scan within the next week and start aspirin 75 mg daily
options.B: Check her blood pressure again after half an hour of rest before deciding on further action
options.C: Call 999 for an emergency ambulance to a hyperacute stroke unit, pre-alerting the hospital
options.D: Make an urgent referral to the neurology outpatient clinic for review within the next two weeks
options.E: Advise her to attend the emergency department by taxi once her symptoms have improved

correct_answer: C. Call 999 for an emergency ambulance to a hyperacute stroke unit, pre-alerting the hospital
why_correct: A new facial droop, arm weakness and speech disturbance with a positive FAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time) screen means acute stroke until proven otherwise, and treatments such as thrombolysis and thrombectomy are time-critical. She should be sent immediately by emergency ambulance, with a pre-alert, to a specialist hyperacute stroke unit rather than being worked up in the community. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, 2022 update.
why_wrong: A. Delayed outpatient imaging would miss the window for reperfusion treatment, and aspirin should not be started before brain imaging has excluded haemorrhage. B. Waiting and re-checking observations wastes time, and blood pressure is not the deciding factor in the prehospital decision. D. An urgent outpatient neurology referral is for stable, non-emergency problems and is far too slow for acute stroke. E. Self-transport after waiting for improvement delays specialist assessment and risks a deteriorating patient travelling without clinical support.
pearl: In suspected stroke, every minute of delay costs brain tissue, so the first action is the emergency call, not a test.
thinking: Sudden face, arm and speech problems  ↓  FAST positive  ↓  treat as acute stroke  ↓  999 and direct to a hyperacute stroke unit  ↓  imaging and reperfusion decisions made there.
exam_trap: Starting aspirin in the surgery before imaging is tempting, but haemorrhage must be excluded first and the priority is transfer.
takeaway: A positive FAST screen means an immediate emergency ambulance to a stroke unit.
notes: Rewritten as a primary-care scenario with the same learning point as the source (suspected stroke needs the acute stroke pathway immediately). Verified against NICE NG128: FAST in the community, immediate admission to a specialist acute stroke unit; aspirin 300 mg only after haemorrhage is excluded, so option A is wrong on two counts. Source stem had no vignette detail; added age, onset time and signs.
Duplicate: live PAQ16162 (generalised tonic-clonic seizure recognition) and NEU015 already cover this learning point.

presentation: Loss of smell after head injury
stem:
A 31-year-old cyclist was knocked off his bike and struck the front of his helmet. He was admitted overnight with a mild head injury and CT of the brain was normal. Two weeks later he tells his GP that food tastes bland and he can no longer smell coffee, although his vision, hearing and facial movements are normal.

Which structure is most likely to have been injured?

options.A: The trigeminal nerve branches supplying the nasal mucosa
options.B: The vestibulocochlear nerve within the petrous temporal bone
options.C: The facial nerve within the facial canal of the temporal bone
options.D: The optic chiasm above the pituitary fossa
options.E: The olfactory nerve fibres crossing the cribriform plate

correct_answer: E. The olfactory nerve fibres crossing the cribriform plate
why_correct: Anosmia after head trauma is typically caused by shearing of the delicate olfactory nerve fibres as they pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, and it can occur even when CT is normal. Taste seems reduced because flavour depends heavily on smell, so a bland taste with normal facial and visual function points to olfactory nerve injury. Source: standard neuroanatomy; NICE NG232, Head injury, 2023 (assessment and complications).
why_wrong: A. Trigeminal branches carry nasal sensation (for example, to irritants), not the sense of smell. B. Vestibulocochlear injury causes hearing loss, tinnitus or vertigo, which he does not have. C. Facial nerve injury causes facial weakness and altered taste from the anterior tongue, but his face moves normally. D. Chiasmal injury would cause visual field loss, which is absent here.
pearl: Anosmia after a frontal blow or fall is a classic sign of cribriform plate injury and may be the only neurological finding.
thinking: Head injury  ↓  loss of smell and bland food  ↓  other cranial nerve functions normal  ↓  shearing of olfactory fibres at the cribriform plate.
exam_trap: Taste complaints can mislead candidates into choosing the facial nerve, but flavour loss usually reflects smell loss.
takeaway: Isolated loss of smell after head trauma points to the olfactory nerve at the cribriform plate.

presentation: Sudden short-lived amnesia in an older adult
stem:
A 64-year-old retired teacher is brought to the emergency department by her husband. While they were gardening an hour ago, after an argument, she suddenly began asking the same questions again and again, such as what day it was and why they were there. She knows her own name and recognises her husband. She has no headache, weakness, speech disturbance or limb jerking, and examination, including gait and cranial nerves, is normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Focal impaired awareness seizure of the temporal lobe
options.B: Transient ischaemic attack in the posterior circulation
options.C: Delirium due to an occult urinary tract infection
options.D: Transient global amnesia, a benign memory syndrome
options.E: Wernicke encephalopathy with early Korsakoff features

correct_answer: D. Transient global amnesia, a benign memory syndrome
why_correct: Transient global amnesia is a sudden loss of the ability to lay down new memories, with repeated questioning and preserved personal identity, alertness and other neurological function. It is often triggered by emotional stress or exertion and settles within hours without treatment. A normal neurological examination and no other deficit make a seizure, TIA or delirium less likely. Source: NHS, Transient global amnesia; Association of British Neurologists, Practical Neurology review of transient global amnesia.
why_wrong: A. A temporal lobe seizure usually causes automatisms, staring or altered awareness in brief episodes, rather than a prolonged isolated amnesia. B. A posterior circulation TIA would usually bring other brainstem or visual symptoms such as vertigo, diplopia or field loss. C. Delirium causes fluctuating attention and disorientation with clouded alertness, not isolated repetitive questioning in an alert patient. E. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome follows heavy alcohol use or malnutrition and causes ataxia, confusion and eye signs, none of which are present.
pearl: Repeated questioning in an otherwise alert patient with a normal examination is the hallmark of transient global amnesia.
thinking: Sudden anterograde amnesia with repetition  ↓  alert, knows who she is  ↓  no focal deficit or seizure features  ↓  transient global amnesia, with reassurance and exclusion of mimics.
exam_trap: Candidates overcall TIA or seizure, but the absence of any focal deficit or positive seizure features favours transient global amnesia.
takeaway: A single episode of repeated questioning and new memory failure with a normal neurological examination is transient global amnesia.
notes: New vignette with a typical emotional trigger (source stem was a bare description). Diagnosis is clinical, benign and self-limiting; atypical features (focal signs, seizure features, very prolonged episodes) should prompt further investigation. No duration threshold is needed for the key. No dedicated NICE guideline exists for TGA, so NHS and Practical Neurology are cited; a reviewer may wish to confirm the citation.

presentation: Parkinson's disease with constipation and reduced smell
stem:
A 74-year-old man was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease two years ago and takes co-beneldopa. He asks his GP about long-standing constipation and a loss of smell that began years before his tremor appeared. He is worried that there may be a second illness. Abdominal examination is normal and he has no weight loss or rectal bleeding.

Which statement best explains these symptoms?

options.A: They are non-motor features of Parkinson's disease that may precede the motor symptoms
options.B: They most likely indicate an additional diagnosis such as colorectal cancer or nasal polyps
options.C: They are adverse effects of co-beneldopa, so the drug should be stopped immediately
options.D: They suggest that the diagnosis is multiple system atrophy rather than Parkinson's disease
options.E: They suggest that Alzheimer's disease has developed alongside his Parkinson's disease

correct_answer: A. They are non-motor features of Parkinson's disease that may precede the motor symptoms
why_correct: Parkinson's disease is not purely a movement disorder; constipation, reduced sense of smell, sleep disturbance, low mood and autonomic problems are recognised non-motor features and may begin years before the tremor or slowness. Because he has no alarm features, these symptoms are best explained by the Parkinson's disease itself and managed symptomatically. Source: NICE NG71, Parkinson's disease in adults, 2017 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: B. New bowel symptoms with alarm features would need investigation, but long-standing symptoms that predate the motor features without red flags are explained by Parkinson's disease. C. The symptoms preceded treatment, and stopping levodopa abruptly risks a dangerous worsening or a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome. D. Multiple system atrophy is suggested by early severe autonomic failure, poor levodopa response and rapid progression, not by these features alone. E. Alzheimer's disease causes progressive memory loss and does not explain constipation or reduced smell in this vignette.
pearl: Reduced sense of smell and constipation can come years before the tremor in Parkinson's disease.
thinking: Parkinson's disease plus constipation and reduced smell  ↓  symptoms predate motor onset and no red flags  ↓  recognised non-motor features  ↓  reassure and treat symptomatically.
exam_trap: Attributing every new symptom to levodopa leads to unsafe stopping of the drug.
takeaway: Non-motor features such as constipation and reduced smell are part of Parkinson's disease and may precede the motor signs.
notes: Source was a bare symptom list; recast as a patient concern. Added alarm-feature safety wording so new bowel symptoms are not reflexively attributed to Parkinson's disease. NICE NG71 lists non-motor problems (sleep, anosmia, depression, autonomic).

stem:
A 38-year-old teacher has had several months of involuntary contractions of her neck muscles that twist her head to the right and tilt it slightly upwards. The posture can be partially relieved by lightly touching her chin. She has no weakness, sensory loss or tremor at rest, and she has taken no antipsychotic or antiemetic drugs.

Which term best describes this movement disorder?

options.A: Tremor
options.B: Dystonia
options.C: Chorea
options.D: Myoclonus
options.E: Tics

correct_answer: B. Dystonia
why_correct: Dystonia is a movement disorder in which sustained or intermittent muscle contractions cause twisting movements and abnormal postures, and focal neck involvement is called cervical dystonia. A sensory trick, such as touching the chin to ease the posture, is characteristic. Source: NHS, Dystonia; Association of British Neurologists teaching on movement disorders.
why_wrong: A. Tremor is a rhythmic oscillation of a body part rather than a sustained twisting posture. C. Chorea consists of irregular, brief, flowing and unpredictable movements that move from one body part to another. D. Myoclonus consists of sudden, brief, shock-like jerks, not sustained postures. E. Tics are repetitive, stereotyped movements or sounds that can be briefly suppressed and are preceded by an urge.
pearl: A sensory trick that eases the posture is a useful bedside clue to dystonia.
thinking: Sustained twisting neck posture  ↓  eased by touching the chin  ↓  not rhythmic, brief or jerky  ↓  dystonia (cervical).
exam_trap: Candidates may pick tremor because the head is moving, but the key feature is the sustained posture.
takeaway: Sustained or intermittent muscle contraction producing twisting movements and abnormal postures is dystonia.
notes: Source options mixed unrelated terms (aphasia, paraesthesia); replaced with movement-disorder terms so distractors are plausible. Added drug history to exclude acute drug-induced dystonia. Single-word options; key is mid-length. Live NEU079/P072 cover drug-induced acute dystonia (treatment), not recognition of dystonia as a term. No NICE guideline for dystonia recognition; NHS page cited.

presentation: Multiple sclerosis with new symptoms lasting days
stem:
A 29-year-old woman has had relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis for three years and is well controlled on disease-modifying treatment. Over the last four days she has developed numbness and clumsiness in her right hand that is gradually worsening. She is afebrile, has no urinary symptoms or recent illness, and has not been exposed to hot weather or exercise.

Which of the following does this pattern most likely represent?

options.A: A pseudo-relapse caused by a hidden urinary infection
options.B: A transient heat-related worsening of old symptoms
options.C: A new episode of functional neurological disorder
options.D: A migraine aura occurring without a headache
options.E: A new acute relapse of her multiple sclerosis

correct_answer: E. A new acute relapse of her multiple sclerosis
why_correct: In multiple sclerosis, new or worsening neurological symptoms that last for more than a day in the absence of infection, fever or another explanation represent a relapse. Her subacute hand symptoms with no fever or triggers fit a relapse, which should be assessed for treatment such as a short course of high-dose corticosteroids. Source: NICE NG220, Multiple sclerosis in adults, 2022.
why_wrong: A. A pseudo-relapse follows infection or fever, and she has neither urinary symptoms nor systemic illness. B. Uhthoff phenomenon causes temporary worsening with heat or exercise that settles on cooling, and she has had no such exposure. C. Functional disorder produces inconsistent signs and should not be assumed in a patient with established demyelination and a progressing deficit. D. A migraine aura usually lasts under an hour and may be followed by headache, rather than persisting and progressing over days.
pearl: New MS symptoms lasting more than a day without infection or heat are a relapse until proven otherwise.
thinking: Known multiple sclerosis  ↓  new deficit over days  ↓  no fever, infection or heat trigger  ↓  acute relapse  ↓  assess for treatment.
exam_trap: Missing a hidden infection can cause a pseudo-relapse, so always look for infection before labelling a relapse.
takeaway: New neurological deficit lasting days in MS, after excluding infection and heat, is a relapse.
notes: New vignette; learning point unchanged. The key does not hinge on a threshold (symptoms last days); the 24-hour definition appears only in the explanation, per NICE NG220. Source distractors (otitis externa, dehydration) replaced with genuine MS mimics (pseudo-relapse, Uhthoff). Live NEU019/NEU104/DS004 test treatment or infection exclusion in worsening symptoms, not recognition of a new episode.
Duplicate: live BX880 (crossed cranial nerve and limb signs, brainstem) tests the same learning point.

stem:
A 62-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes complains of numb feet and says he falls when washing his face in the dark. At the bedside he stands steadily with his feet together and eyes open, but he sways markedly and nearly falls when asked to close his eyes. Power in his legs is normal, but vibration sense and joint position sense are reduced at the toes.

What does this finding most strongly indicate?

options.A: A lesion in the cerebellar vermis causing truncal ataxia
options.B: Loss of joint position sense from sensory neuropathy
options.C: Upper motor neurone weakness affecting both legs
options.D: A lower motor neurone lesion of the lumbar roots
options.E: Dysfunction of the cerebellar hemisphere on one side

correct_answer: B. Loss of joint position sense from sensory neuropathy
why_correct: A positive Romberg test, where balance worsens when vision is removed, indicates loss of proprioceptive (or vestibular) input, because the eyes normally compensate for the missing sensory information. With reduced vibration and joint position sense in a diabetic patient, the picture fits a sensory ataxia from peripheral neuropathy. Source: standard clinical neurology examination teaching (Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine); NICE CKS, Diabetes type 2.
why_wrong: A. Vermis lesions cause truncal instability that is present with the eyes open as well, so they do not produce a Romberg-positive result. C. Upper motor neurone weakness gives spasticity and brisk reflexes with weakness, and his power is normal. D. A lower motor neurone lesion gives wasting, weakness and reduced reflexes, not selective position-sense loss. E. Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause limb ataxia and unsteadiness with the eyes open, so closing the eyes does not make them markedly worse.
pearl: If balance is fine with eyes open and fails with eyes closed, think of a proprioceptive (dorsal column or peripheral nerve) problem.
thinking: Stable eyes open, unstable eyes closed  ↓  reduced vibration and joint position sense  ↓  proprioceptive loss  ↓  sensory ataxia from neuropathy.
exam_trap: A cerebellar cause is tempting because of the unsteadiness, but cerebellar ataxia is not corrected by vision.
takeaway: A positive Romberg test indicates impaired proprioception or vestibular function, not cerebellar or motor weakness.
notes: New clinical vignette adding a diabetic neuropathy context and sensory findings; source distractors (aphasia, facial palsy) were irrelevant and have been replaced with plausible localisation errors. Romberg tests dorsal column/peripheral proprioceptive (and vestibular) function. No figures involved.

presentation: Knee extension weakness and L3-L4 root
stem:
A 58-year-old man has had two weeks of pain across the front of his thigh and inner shin. On examination he cannot fully straighten his right knee against resistance, the right knee jerk is reduced, and the ankle jerk and ankle movements are normal. MRI is arranged to look for nerve root compression.

Which nerve root is most likely to be affected?

options.A: L5 root, as in a typical sciatic-type disc prolapse
options.B: L3 and L4 roots, supplying the quadriceps
options.C: S1 root, supplying the calf muscles
options.D: S2 root, supplying the hamstrings
options.E: L1 root, supplying the hip flexor muscles

correct_answer: B. L3 and L4 roots, supplying the quadriceps
why_correct: Straightening the knee depends on the quadriceps, which is supplied by the femoral nerve from the L3 and L4 roots, and the knee jerk is mediated by the same roots. Weak knee extension with a reduced knee jerk and normal ankle findings therefore localises to L3-L4. Source: Standard myotome and reflex levels, Medical Research Council scale and UK undergraduate clinical neurology teaching.
why_wrong: A. L5 mainly controls ankle and big-toe dorsiflexion and hip abduction, and does not explain the weak knee extension or the reduced knee jerk. C. S1 supplies plantarflexion and the ankle jerk, which are normal here. D. The hamstrings bend the knee rather than straighten it, so S2 does not fit. E. L1 contributes to hip flexion and groin sensation, not to the quadriceps.
pearl: Knee jerk is L3-L4 and ankle jerk is S1-S2; matching the reflex to the weak movement fixes the level.
thinking: Weak knee extension  ↓  quadriceps / femoral nerve  ↓  knee jerk reduced  ↓  root level L3-L4
exam_trap: Choosing L5 because it is the commonest lumbar root in sciatica, when the weakness is at the knee and the ankle examination is normal.
takeaway: Knee extension and the knee jerk are L3-L4; ankle dorsiflexion is L4-L5 and the ankle jerk is S1.
notes: Source was a one-line recall item; rebuilt as a root-localisation vignette (root compression) rather than a nerve-name question, so it does not repeat BX643 (femoral nerve after pelvic surgery). Source key L3-L4 is correct. No guideline exists for myotome levels; citation is standard teaching.
sources: Standard myotome/reflex tables (MRC); clinical neurological examination teaching

notes: Duplicate: live BX173 (wasting/fasciculations with reduced reflexes = LMN), BX637 and BX641 already test LMN vs UMN signs.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman with a three-year history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis develops numbness and clumsiness of her left hand over four days. She has no fever or urinary symptoms. Over the next six weeks the symptoms improve substantially without full recovery of fine finger movements.

Which term best describes this episode?

options.A: Clinically isolated syndrome
options.B: Relapse of her multiple sclerosis
options.C: Pseudorelapse from infection
options.D: Primary progressive course
options.E: Functional neurological disorder episode

correct_answer: B. Relapse of her multiple sclerosis
why_correct: A relapse in multiple sclerosis is a new or worsening neurological episode that develops over days, lasts longer than a brief fluctuation, occurs without fever or infection, and is followed by full or partial recovery. This woman's established diagnosis, afebrile subacute onset and later improvement fit that pattern. Source: NICE NG220, Multiple sclerosis in adults: management, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Clinically isolated syndrome describes the first demyelinating episode before multiple sclerosis is diagnosed, and she already has the diagnosis. C. A pseudorelapse is a temporary worsening of old symptoms triggered by infection or heat, but she has no fever or infective symptoms. D. A primary progressive course shows steady worsening from onset without distinct episodes and recovery. E. Nothing suggests a functional cause, and an established demyelinating disease explains the deficit.
pearl: After a presumed relapse, always look for infection or fever first, because pseudorelapses mimic relapses.
thinking: Known relapsing-remitting MS  ↓  new symptoms over days  ↓  no infection or fever  ↓  partial recovery = relapse
exam_trap: Calling it a clinically isolated syndrome, which is only used for the first episode before the diagnosis is made.
takeaway: A relapse is new or worsening MS symptoms over days, without infection, usually followed by recovery.
notes: One-line term-recall item rebuilt as a vignette. Wording avoids any duration threshold (NG220 uses more than 24 hours and 30 days from the last relapse; not needed for the key). Does not repeat NEU019 (relapse treatment) or DS004 (excluding infection first).

stem:
A 66-year-old man is recently diagnosed with Parkinson's disease after developing a resting tremor and slowness of movement. He asks his GP whether other problems he noticed for years before the tremor could be part of the same condition.

Which of his earlier symptoms is a recognised non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease?

options.A: Episodes of pleuritic chest pain on deep breathing
options.B: Recurrent painful swelling of the knee joints
options.C: A progressively reduced sense of smell
options.D: Gradually worsening difficulty with night vision
options.E: Frequent unprovoked nosebleeds from one nostril

correct_answer: C. A progressively reduced sense of smell
why_correct: Parkinson's disease has many non-motor features, and a reduced sense of smell (hyposmia) is among the commonest and may precede the tremor by years. Others include constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, low mood and autonomic problems, which is why symptoms outside movement should be asked about. Source: NICE NG71, Parkinson's disease in adults, 2017.
why_wrong: A. Pleuritic chest pain suggests a pleural or pericardial problem and is not part of Parkinson's disease. B. Recurrent joint swelling points to an inflammatory or crystal arthropathy. D. Poor night vision suggests retinal or vitamin A-related disease, not Parkinson's disease. E. Unilateral recurrent epistaxis needs a local nasal cause to be sought.
pearl: Hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder and low mood can precede the motor features of Parkinson's disease.
thinking: Parkinson's disease diagnosed  ↓  ask about non-motor symptoms  ↓  smell loss, constipation, sleep disorder, mood  ↓  choose the recognised feature
exam_trap: Thinking Parkinson's disease only affects movement, so that a loss of smell is dismissed as an unrelated problem.
takeaway: Parkinson's disease has recognised non-motor features such as hyposmia, constipation and sleep disturbance.

stem:
A 35-year-old man with known epilepsy has a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure at home. When paramedics arrive, his left arm and leg are weak. His weakness gradually improves over several hours and has fully resolved by the next morning. A CT head scan is normal.

What is the most likely explanation for the weakness?

options.A: Right middle cerebral artery TIA
options.B: Hemiplegic migraine with aura
options.C: Functional neurological weakness
options.D: Todd's paresis (postictal paralysis)
options.E: Acute demyelination of the right hemisphere

correct_answer: D. Todd's paresis (postictal paralysis)
why_correct: Temporary focal weakness lasting minutes to hours after a seizure is Todd's paresis (postictal paralysis), thought to reflect neuronal exhaustion in the area that seized. It resolves spontaneously, and a normal scan with a clear temporal relationship to a witnessed seizure supports it. Source: NICE NG217, Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, 2022.
why_wrong: A. A transient ischaemic attack can cause temporary weakness, but here the weakness began straight after a convulsion and evolved gradually, which points to a postictal cause. B. Hemiplegic migraine follows a headache and aura rather than a generalised convulsion. C. Functional weakness is a diagnosis of exclusion and is not suggested by a witnessed seizure in a known epileptic. E. Demyelination evolves over days and does not resolve within hours.
pearl: Todd's paresis lasts from minutes to a day or so; persistent weakness should prompt imaging for stroke or other structural causes.
thinking: Known epilepsy and witnessed seizure  ↓  hemiparesis afterwards  ↓  improves over hours  ↓  Todd's paresis
exam_trap: Labelling post-seizure weakness as a stroke or TIA without recognising the postictal pattern.
takeaway: Transient focal weakness after a seizure that resolves over hours is Todd's paresis.
notes: Source distractors were unrelated diagnoses; replaced with plausible competing causes of transient hemiweakness. Plan puts the key at D. NG217 does not name Todd's paresis explicitly; citation is for the epilepsy context, the term is standard neurology teaching.
